Population attributable fraction

Source: R/pollution.R
attrfrac.Rd

The share of all cases in a population that is due to an exposure: the fraction that would not occur if the exposure were removed and nothing else changed. It combines how strongly the exposure raises risk (the relative risk) with how common it is (the prevalence); multiplied by the number of cases it gives the attributable cases, as polbrdn does.

Usage

attrfrac(rr, expoprev, rrlo = NULL, rrup = NULL)

Arguments

rr

Relative risk among the exposed, a single finite positive number. A relative risk below 1 gives a negative fraction (a protective exposure); 0, negative, infinite and missing values are errors.

expoprev

Proportion of the population exposed, in [0, 1].

rrlo, rrup

Optional confidence limits of rr; when both are given the fraction carries the limits that the same formula gives at them (Levin's formula is monotone in the relative risk, so the interval of the fraction is the image of the interval of the risk).

Value

A single number, the attributable fraction: in [0, 1) for rr >= 1, negative for a protective exposure. When the limits were given it carries an attribute ci, a named numeric vector (lower, upper).

Details

Levin's formula (Levin 1953; Rothman, Greenland and Lash 2008, chapter 5): $$PAF = p (RR - 1) / (1 + p (RR - 1)),$$ with \(p\) the proportion exposed. With everyone exposed it is \(1 - 1/RR\). It assumes the relative risk is causal and unconfounded and that removing the exposure changes nothing else. A relative risk below 1 gives a negative fraction (the exposure protects).

When both confidence limits of the RR are given, the fraction's limits are the formula applied to them: the formula increases with the RR, so the interval of the fraction is the image of the interval of the risk. Refusals: an rr or limit that is not a single finite positive number (logical values included), a prevalence outside \([0, 1]\), only one of the two limits, or limits that do not enclose rr.

References

Rothman, K. J., Greenland, S. and Lash, T. L. (2008). Modern Epidemiology, 3rd ed., chapter 5. Levin, M. L. (1953). The occurrence of lung cancer in man. Acta Unio Internationalis Contra Cancrum 9, 531-541.

See also

crfpm25 for a relative risk from a concentration, polbrdn for the attributable cases.

Examples

attrfrac(1.5, 0.4)
#> [1] 0.1666667
attrfrac(2, 1)      # everyone exposed: 1 - 1/RR
#> [1] 0.5

# With the confidence limits of the relative risk.
paf <- attrfrac(1.08, 1, rrlo = 1.06, rrup = 1.09)
attr(paf, "ci")
#>      lower      upper 
#> 0.05660377 0.08256881 

# A protective exposure gives a negative fraction.
attrfrac(0.8, 0.5)
#> [1] -0.1111111

# A prevalence above 1 is refused.
try(attrfrac(1.5, 40))
#> Error : expoprev must be in [0,1]; got 40
